intro: Lazur is an AI assistant for project managers on Mac. It sees your screen while you hold the shortcut, answers out loud, and drafts the text you need for status reports, follow ups and risk notes. This page covers where a project manager's day goes, which jobs are worth handing off, and one worked example in PowerPoint and Excel.

blocks.text: Where a project manager's day actually goes

Most of your day does not go to planning. Asana says about 60% of a person's time at work goes to work about work. That covers communicating about tasks and repeating work that already exists. The number comes from Asana's own research, so read it as one company's view. It still matches how many project managers feel on a Tuesday afternoon.

Microsoft's data points the same way from a different angle. Its 2023 Work Trend Index covered 31,000 workers in 31 markets, and it tracked their Microsoft 365 use. Across those apps, 57% of time went to communicating through meetings, chat and email. The other 43% went to creating. Excel alone took 18% of total time, and PowerPoint took 8%. These are averages for office workers, not project managers, so use them as direction rather than a precise count.
Who this assistant is for

Project managers, PMO analysts and project coordinators share the same core job. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics describes project management specialists as people who coordinate the budget, schedule, staffing and other details of a project. Its May 2025 median pay was $102,320 a year. Projected growth from 2025 to 2035 is 7%, with about 76,500 openings a year on average.

If you run projects from a Mac, your tools are spreadsheets, decks and chat, and your hours are split across them. A helper that works in whatever app is open fits that pattern better than a dashboard you have to visit. The value is not one big feature. It is the small answers you no longer hunt for.
What an AI assistant for project managers should do on your Mac

A useful assistant does three things well. It answers where something is. It walks you through steps you rarely take. It drafts text you can send. It should do all three in the app you already have open, because your hour may cross Excel, Slack, Mail, Calendar and PowerPoint. Lazur is built around that pattern. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud.

items: Point: ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.
Guide: ask how to do something, and Lazur walks you one click at a time, waiting for each click.
Draft: ask for a status line, a follow up or a risk note, and Lazur writes it as text.
Dictate: hold fn and speak clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app.
Research: send a question to a background job. It runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and returns a summary and a report.

blocks.text: Lazur does not click buttons, edit your files or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app. That limit shapes how you use it. You make the change. Lazur saves you the hunt for the button and the first draft of the message.
Status reports without the Friday scramble

A weekly status report is three jobs in one. You read the tracker, you decide what is on track, and you write a few honest sentences. The reading part eats the most time, so start there. Open the tracker, hold ⌥ ⌘ over a Status cell, and ask: 'What does this amber color mean?' Lazur points at the cell and answers out loud from what is on screen.

The judgment stays with you. Lazur cannot know that the vendor promised a fix on Monday. It can turn the facts you give it into clean text. Say the facts plainly: 'Scope is on track. The vendor slipped delivery to the second week. Timing is amber because of extra testing. Draft three lines for the steering group.' Lazur types the draft at your cursor. Read every line, especially any date, cost or name.

blocks.text: Look at the right column. Every row ends with a decision that belongs to you. A project manager owns the schedule, the budget and the people. Lazur speeds up the search and the typing. It does not own the call.
Follow ups and call notes you do not have to type

Most project managers leave a call with a list in their head. The follow up then waits until the end of the day, and details slip. Hold fn, speak the list in plain words, and release the key. Dictation writes formatted text at the cursor, so the words land where you are typing, in Slack or Mail. Names matter here. Add client names and team codes to your personal dictionary so they stay spelled right.

blocks.title: Rough first, clean second
blocks.text: Dictate the messy version first, then hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to tighten it for the team. A rough pass and a clean pass beat one long try at a perfect message.

If you want to see how much faster speaking is for you than typing, try the [speaking versus typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test). The result tells you which tasks to hand to your voice first. Start with follow ups and status drafts, since those are the messages you write most often.
Excel and Google Sheets: find the cell, not the menu

Excel is where much of a project lives. Microsoft's data gives it 18% of total time across its apps. Most of that time is not spent building models. It goes to finding a column, a filter or the rule that turned a cell red. Lazur helps most in those moments. It sees the sheet while you hold the shortcut, points at what you ask about, and explains it in plain words.

Google Sheets works the same way in Chrome. For the menu steps on a routine job, the guide on [freezing the top row in Google Sheets](/how-to/freeze-the-top-row-in-google-sheets) is a short start. For a full tracker setup, read the [Google Sheets page for project managers](/for/project-managers/google-sheets). Excel users can start with the [Excel page for project managers](/for/project-managers/excel).

Here is a common case. A risk column shows colors, but nobody on the team agrees on the rule. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask: 'Which rule colors this cell?' In Excel, the rule lives under Home > Conditional Formatting > Manage Rules. Lazur points you there and explains the rule. Changing it is your job. Menus move between versions, so check the menu bar on your copy.
PowerPoint: steering decks that do not eat your afternoon

PowerPoint took 8% of total time in Microsoft's 2023 data. For a project manager, that slice usually means updating the same few slides every cycle. The slow part is finding the place in the deck, not the writing. Hold ⌥ ⌘ over a slide and ask where the speaker notes live. Lazur points at the spot. You can follow up with [how to add speaker notes in PowerPoint](/how-to/add-speaker-notes-in-powerpoint).

Use drafting for slide titles. Say what the slide must show: 'The schedule slipped a week, and the fix is in place.' Ask for three titles that state the point, not the topic. Pick one and type it in. A title that states the point reads faster for a steering group than 'Schedule update.'
A Thursday before the steering committee

Here is how a worked day can run. At 09:00 you open the tracker and ask Lazur to explain any new red cells. At 10:15 you dictate the vendor call notes into a draft email. At 11:00 you ask for three status lines. At 14:00 you ask for a walkthrough on adding a dropdown to the risk sheet. Before you leave, you set a reminder to send the deck.

Notice what Lazur did not do. It did not decide the status. It did not send the email. It did not change the sheet. Each step saved a search, a rewrite or a menu hunt. The decisions and the sending stayed with you, which is how it should work.
Mistakes that cost project managers time

items: Asking for a status before checking the facts. Lazur drafts from what you say and what is on screen. Bad inputs make smooth, wrong drafts.
Sending a draft without reading it. Check every date, cost and name, since those are the lines people quote back to you.
Sharing client or project data that your employer does not allow in AI tools. Check the rules before you hold the shortcut.
Expecting Lazur to click. Ask for the steps, then make the click yourself.
Holding the shortcut over a screen full of private material. Close the windows you do not need before you ask.

faq.question: What is an AI assistant for project managers on a Mac?
faq.answer: It is a tool that answers questions about what is on your screen, points at things, and drafts text. Lazur works this way on a Mac. You hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask and hold fn to dictate. It works in whichever app you have open, and it is not a plugin for any of them.

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Excel, Google Sheets and Slack?
faq.answer: It works alongside them. Lazur sees the screen only while you hold the shortcut, points at controls, explains them, and types drafts at your cursor. It is not an add-in, and it has no partnership with any app maker.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons or change my tracker for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points, explains and guides. When you ask how to do something, it walks you one click at a time and waits for each click. You make every change yourself.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with client or project data?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. When you hold ⌥ ⌘, Lazur sends the audio and a screenshot to AI providers to answer. Lazur says these are not stored, and content is not used to train AI models. This page makes no compliance claim, so check with your company.

faq.question: Does Lazur record meetings?
faq.answer: Meeting recording is not on Lazur's feature list. Its features are voice questions, dictation, everyday actions like timers and Calendar events, research in Chrome tabs, and memory of what you asked. Dictate your follow up after the call instead.

faq.question: Is there a Windows version of Lazur?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: How do I try Lazur without paying?
faq.answer: There is a Pro trial with no credit card. It starts when you first open the app. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for current plans before you decide.

faq.question: Does Lazur remember my project details?
faq.answer: Lazur keeps memory of what you asked and did, and that memory stays on your Mac. Treat it like any other notes on your machine, and clear what you do not need.

painPoints.title: Work about work crowds out planning

painPoints.title: Tracker questions interrupt the day
painPoints.text: A teammate asks what a color means. Someone else asks where a filter went. Each small question costs a minute and breaks the thread of your own work.

painPoints.title: Follow ups die in Slack threads
painPoints.text: The call ends with five action items in your head. By the time you type them, one is wrong and another is missing. Speaking the list at once keeps it accurate.

painPoints.title: Deck updates take an afternoon
painPoints.text: Most of the time goes into finding the slide, the speaker notes and the right layout. Writing the new point often takes a few minutes.
